title: حِكَايَةُ الْمَلِكِ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ
part: Night 80 · King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 470–471 (Night 80, continuing directly from nights-79), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 80 continues the tale of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān. The second of the five learned slave-girls kisses the ground before the king and begins her speech with sayings attributed to Luqmān, the Prophet and the Qurʾān on the heart, anger, greed and the remembrance of God, then a short poem; she turns to the reports of the ascetics, Abū Dharr and Thābit al-Bunānī, until dawn cuts Shahrazād off. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الْمَوْفِيَهُ الثَّمَانِينَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-mawfiyatu al-thamānīna
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the completing-one, the eighty,
sentences.i: And when it was the eightieth night,
sentences.n: The print has المثمانين, a misprint for الثمانين, corrected here.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدَأَنَّ الْوَزِيرَ دَنْدَانَ قَالَ لِضَوْءِ الْمَكَانِ ثُمَّ تَأَخَّرَتِ الْجَارِيَةُ الْأُولَى وَتَقَدَّمَتِ الثَّانِيَةُ وَقَبَّلَتِ الْأَرْضَ بَيْنَ يَدَىِ الْمَلِكِ وَالِدِكَ سَبْعَ مَرَّاتٍ ثُمَّ قَالَتْ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīda anna al-wazīra dandāna qāla li-ḍawʾi al-makāni thumma taʾakhkharati al-jāriyatu al-ūlā wa-taqaddamati al-thāniyatu wa-qabbalati al-arḍa bayna yadayi al-maliki wālidika sabʿa marrātin thumma qālat
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O king the happy, that the vizier Dandān said to Ḍawʾ al-Makān: Then the first slave-girl drew back and the second came forward, and kissed the earth between the hands of the king, your father, seven times, then she said:
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the vizier Dandān said to Ḍawʾ al-Makān: Then the first slave-girl stepped back and the second came forward and kissed the ground seven times before the king, your father, and said:
sentences.n: The print runs أن into the word before it (السعيدان, “the happy — that”); it is read as two words. بين يدي الملك والدك is printed with no genitive link between “king” and “your father”; read as “the king, your father”.

sentences.t: قَالَ لُقْمَانُ لِابْنِهِ ثَلٰثَةٌ لَا تُعْرَفُ إِلَّا في ثَلٰثَةِ مَوَاطِنَ لَايُعْرَفُ الْحَلِيمُ إِلَّا عِنْدَ الْغَضَبِ وَلَا الشُّجَاعُ إِلَّا عِنْدَ الْحَرْبِ وَلَا أَخُوكَ إِلَّا عِنْدَ حَاجَتِكَ إِلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: qāla luqmānu li-ibnihi thalāthatun lā tuʿrafu illā fī thalāthati mawāṭina lā yuʿrafu al-ḥalīmu illā ʿinda al-ghaḍabi wa-lā al-shujāʿu illā ʿinda al-ḥarbi wa-lā akhūka illā ʿinda ḥājatika ilayhi
sentences.l: Luqmān said to his son: Three are not known except in three places: the forbearing-one is not known except at anger, nor the brave-one except at war, nor your brother except at your need of him.
sentences.i: Luqmān said to his son: Three men are known only in three places: the patient man only in anger, the brave man only in war, and your brother only when you have need of him.
sentences.n: The print spells ثلاثة as ثلثة, without the alif; the vocalisation reads it as ثلاثة. لا يعرف is printed run together (لايعرف).

sentences.t: وَقِيلَ إِنَّ الظَّالِمَ نَادِمٌ وَإِنْ مَدَحَهُ النَّاسُ وَالْمَظْلُومَ سَلِيمٌ وَإِنْ ذَمَّهُ النَّاسُ
sentences.tr: wa-qīla inna al-ẓālima nādimun wa-in madaḥahu al-nāsu wa-al-maẓlūma salīmun wa-in dhammahu al-nāsu
sentences.l: And it was said: Indeed the wrongdoer is regretful even if the people praise him, and the wronged-one is safe even if the people blame him.
sentences.i: It is said that the wrongdoer is full of regret even though people praise him, and the wronged man is safe even though people blame him.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى وَلَا تَحْسَبَنَّ الَّذِينَ يَفْرَحُونَ بِمَا أَتَوْا وَيُحِبُّونَ أَنْ يُحْمَدُوا بِمَا لَمْ يَفْعَلُوا فَلَا تَحْسَبَنَّهُمْ بِمَفَازَةٍ مِنَ الْعَذَابِ وَلَهُمْ عَذَابٌ أَلِيمٌ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla allāhu taʿālā wa-lā taḥsabanna alladhīna yafraḥūna bi-mā ataw wa-yuḥibbūna an yuḥmadū bi-mā lam yafʿalū fa-lā taḥsabannahum bi-mafāzatin mina al-ʿadhābi wa-lahum ʿadhābun alīmun
sentences.l: And God, exalted is He, said: And do not think those who rejoice in what they have brought, and love to be praised for what they have not done — do not think them in an escape from the torment; and for them is a painful torment.
sentences.i: God Most High said: “Do not think that those who rejoice in what they have done, and love to be praised for what they have not done, are in any escape from the punishment; for them there is a painful punishment.”
sentences.n: A Qurʾānic quotation (the sense of Āl ʿImrān 3:188). بمفازة: بِـ, “in, within” — “in an escape”.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ عَلَيْهِ الصَّلٰوةُ وَالسَّلَامُ إِنَّمَا الْأَعْمَالُ بِالنِّيَّاتِ وَإِنَّمَا لِكُلِّ امْرِئٍ مَا نَوَى
sentences.tr: wa-qāla ʿalayhi al-ṣalātu wa-al-salāmu innamā al-aʿmālu bi-al-niyyāti wa-innamā li-kulli imriʾin mā nawā
sentences.l: And he, upon him be the prayer and the peace, said: Only the deeds are by the intentions, and only for every man is what he intended.
sentences.i: And the Prophet, peace and blessings upon him, said: “Deeds are judged only by intentions, and each man has only what he intended.”
sentences.n: “He, upon him be the prayer and the peace” is the Prophet Muḥammad; the print spells الصلاة as الصلوة.

sentences.t: وَأَيْضًا قَالَ عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ إِنَّ فِى الْجَسَدِ لَمُضْغَةً إِذَا صَلَحَتْ صَلَحَ الْجَسَدُ كُلُّهُ وَإِذَا فَسَدَتْ فَسَدَ الْجَسَدُ كُلُّهُ أَلَا وَهِيَ الْقَلْبُ
sentences.tr: wa-ayḍan qāla ʿalayhi al-salāmu inna fī al-jasadi la-muḍghatan idhā ṣalaḥat ṣalaḥa al-jasadu kulluhu wa-idhā fasadat fasada al-jasadu kulluhu alā wa-hiya al-qalbu
sentences.l: And also he, upon him be the peace, said: Indeed in the body there is a morsel; when it is sound, the body, all of it, is sound, and when it is corrupt, the body, all of it, is corrupt; now, it is the heart.
sentences.i: And he, peace be upon him, also said: “In the body there is a morsel of flesh; when it is sound the whole body is sound, and when it is corrupt the whole body is corrupt. That is the heart.”
sentences.n: لَمُضْغَةً: لَـ, the emphatic “indeed”, on the predicate after إنّ.

sentences.t: وَأَعْجَبُ مَافِى الْإِنْسَانِ قَلْبُهُ لِأَنَّ بِهِ زِمَامَ أَمْرِءٍ فَإِنْ هَاجَ بِهِ الطَّمَعُ أَهْلَكَهُ الْحِرْصُ وَإِنْ مَلَكَهُ الْأَسَى قَتَلَهُ الْأَسَفُ وَإِنْ عَظُمَ عِنْدَهُ الْغَضَبُ اشْتَدَّ بِهِ الْعَطَبُ وَإِنْ سَعِدَ بِالرِّضَا أَمِنَ مِنَ السَّخَطِ
sentences.tr: wa-aʿjabu mā fī al-insāni qalbuhu li-anna bihi zimāma amrihi fa-in hāja bihi al-ṭamaʿu ahlakahu al-ḥirṣu wa-in malakahu al-asā qatalahu al-asafu wa-in ʿaẓuma ʿindahu al-ghaḍabu ishtadda bihi al-ʿaṭabu wa-in saʿida bi-al-riḍā amina mina al-sakhaṭi
sentences.l: And the most wondrous of what is in the human is his heart, because by it is the rein of a man; so if greed stirs in it, avidity destroys him, and if grief possesses him, sorrow kills him, and if anger grows great in him, ruin is strong upon him, and if he is made happy by contentment, he is safe from displeasure.
sentences.i: The most wonderful thing in a human being is his heart, for the reins of a man are in it. If greed stirs in it, avidity destroys him; if grief takes hold of it, sorrow kills him; if anger swells in it, ruin comes hard upon him; and if he is made happy by contentment, he is safe from discontent.
sentences.n: The print has زمام امرء, “the rein of a man”, with a bare hamza; vocalised as أمرِءٍ. بِـ in بِهِ (“by it”) is the instrument; in اشتد به, “upon him”.

sentences.t: وَإِنْ نَالَهُ الْخَوْفُ شَغَلَهُ الْحُزْنُ وَإِنْ أَصَابَتْهُ مُصِيبَةٌ ضَمِنَهُ الْجَزَعُ وَإِنِ اسْتَفَادَ مَالًا رُبَّمَا اشْتَغَلَ بِهِ عَنْ ذِكْرِ رَبِّهِ وَإِنْ غَصَّتْهُ فَاقَةٌ أَشْغَلَهُ الْهَمُّ وَإِنْ أَجْهَدَهُ الْجَزَعُ أَقْعَدَهُ الضَّعْفُ فَعَلَى كُلِّ حَالَةٍ لَاصَلَاحَ لَهُ إِلَّا بِذِكْرِ اللَّهِ وَاشْتِغَالِهِ بِمَا فِيهِ تَحْصِيلُ مَعَاشِهِ وَصَلَاحُ مَعَادِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-in nālahu al-khawfu shaghalahu al-ḥuznu wa-in aṣābathu muṣībatun ḍaminahu al-jazaʿu wa-ini istafāda mālan rubbamā ishtaghala bihi ʿan dhikri rabbihi wa-in ghaṣṣathu fāqatun ashghalahu al-hammu wa-in ajhadahu al-jazaʿu aqʿadahu al-ḍaʿfu fa-ʿalā kulli ḥālatin lā ṣalāḥa lahu illā bi-dhikri allāhi wa-ishtighālihi bi-mā fīhi taḥṣīlu maʿāshihi wa-ṣalāḥu maʿādihi
sentences.l: And if fear reaches him, sadness occupies him; and if a calamity strikes him, impatience takes him in charge; and if he gains wealth, perhaps he is busied with it from the remembrance of his Lord; and if want chokes him, worry busies him; and if impatience wears him out, weakness sets him down; so in every state there is no soundness for him except in the remembrance of God and in his being busied with what holds the gaining of his livelihood and the soundness of his return.
sentences.i: If fear reaches him, sorrow occupies him; if calamity strikes him, impatience seizes him; if he gains wealth, he may be so busy with it that he forgets his Lord; if want chokes him, worry preoccupies him; and if impatience wears him out, weakness lays him low. So in every state there is no well-being for him except in the remembrance of God, and in devoting himself to what brings him his livelihood and the well-being of his afterlife.
sentences.n: The print runs لا صلاح together (لاصلاح). ضمنه الجزع is obscure (literally “impatience guarantees / includes him”); read as “takes him in charge”, tentatively. اشغله is printed without the second shaghala sense clear; read “busies”.

sentences.t: وَقِيلَ لِبَعْضِ الْعُلَمَاءِ مَنْ أَسَرُّ النَّاسِ حَالًا قَالَ مَنْ غَلَبَتْ شَهْوَتَهُ مُرُوَّتُهُ وَبَعُدَتْ فِى الْمَعَالِي هِمَّتُهُ فَاتَّسَعَتْ مَعْرِفَتُهُ وَضَاقَتْ مَعْذِرَتُهُ
sentences.tr: wa-qīla li-baʿḍi al-ʿulamāʾi man asarru al-nāsi ḥālan qāla man ghalabat shahwatahu murūʾatuhu wa-baʿudat fī al-maʿālī himmatuhu fa-ttasaʿat maʿrifatuhu wa-ḍāqat maʿdhiratuhu
sentences.l: And it was said to one of the learned: Who is the most delighted of the people in state? He said: He whose manliness has overcome his desire, and whose aspiration is far in the heights, so his knowledge widens and his excuse narrows.
sentences.i: Someone asked a learned man, “Who is the happiest of men in his condition?” He said, “The one whose manliness has overcome his desire, whose aspiration reaches far toward the heights, so that his knowledge grows wide and his room for excuses grows narrow.”
sentences.n: The print has غلبت شهوته مروته with شهوته as if object and مروته as subject; read as “his manliness overcame his desire”, which is the sense. أسرّ is printed with shadda; read as أسَرّ, “more delighted”.

sentences.t: وَمَا أَحْسَنَ مَا قَالَهُ قَ———سٌ
sentences.tr: wa-mā aḥsana mā qālahu q———s
sentences.l: And how fine is what he said, q———s:
sentences.i: And how well he put it, q———s:
sentences.n: The last word is stretched across the line with filler dashes (ق———س), and the letters between are not printed. It may be a poet’s name (Qays?) or a shortened word; it is left as printed and not guessed at.

sentences.t:
وَإِنِّي لَاغْنَى النَّاسِ عَنْ مُتَكَلِّفٍ * يَرَى النَّاسَ اَضْلًا لَاوَمَاهُوَ مُهْتَدِي
وَمَا الْمَالُ وَالْاَخْلَاقُ اِلَّا مَعَارَةٌ * فَكُلُّ بِمَا يُخْفِيهِ فِي الصَّدْرِ مُرْتَدِي
اِذَا مَا اَتَيْتَ الْاَمْرَ مِنْ غَيْرِ بَابِهِ * ضَلَلْتَ وَاِنْ تَدْخُلْ مِنَ الْبَابِ تَهْتَدِي
sentences.tr:
wa-innī la-aghnā al-nāsi ʿan mutakallifin * yarā al-nāsa aḍlan lā wa-mā huwa muhtadī
wa-mā al-mālu wa-al-akhlāqu illā maʿāratun * fa-kullun bi-mā yukhfīhi fī al-ṣadri murtadī
idhā mā ataytā al-amra min ghayri bābihi * ḍalalta wa-in tadkhul mina al-bābi tahtadī
sentences.l:
And indeed I am the most free of people from one who strains, * who sees the people as an error, and he is not himself guided.
And wealth and character are only a loan, * so each wears what he hides in the breast.
When you come to a matter from other than its door, * you go astray; and if you enter by the door, you are guided.
sentences.i:
I am the least needy of men toward the man who strains for effect, who thinks all others in error and is not himself well-guided.
Wealth and character are only borrowed; each man wears what he hides in his breast.
If you come to a matter by any way but its door you go astray; enter by the door and you will find your way.
sentences.n: Verse copied exactly as the edition prints it, marks and all. Line 1 is obscure: اضلا لاوماهو is printed run together and read as أضلُّ، لا وما هو مهتدي; the translation is tentative. معارة (line 2) is read as عارية, “a loan”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْجَارِيَةَ قَالَتْ وَأَمَّا أَخْبَارُ الزَّاهِدِينَ فَقَلٰ هِشَامُ بْنُ بِشْرَقَاتٍ لِعُمَرَ بْنِ عُبَيْدٍ مَا حَقِيقَةُ الزُّهْدِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-jāriyata qālat wa-ammā akhbāru al-zāhidīna fa-qalā hishāmu bnu bishraqātin li-ʿumara bni ʿubaydin mā ḥaqīqatu al-zuhdi
sentences.l: Then the slave-girl said: And as for the reports of the ascetics, he said — Hishām ibn Bishraqāt said to ʿUmar ibn ʿUbayd: What is the reality of asceticism?
sentences.i: Then the slave-girl said: As for the reports of the ascetics, Hishām ibn Bishr said to ʿUmar ibn ʿUbayd, “What is the true nature of asceticism?”
sentences.n: The print sets the verb twice (فقل قل); the second is dropped here.

sentences.t: فَقَلٰ لِي قَدْ بَيَّنَهُ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ فِي قَوْلِهِ الزَّاهِدُ مَنْ لَمْ يَنْسَ الْغَبْرَ وَالْبَلَاءَ وَآثَرَ مَايَبْقَى عَلَى مَا يَفْنَى وَلَمْ يَعُدَّ غَدًا مِنْ أَيَّامِهِ وَعَلَّ نَفْسَهُ فِي الْمَوْتَى
sentences.tr: fa-qalā lī qad bayyanahu rasūlu allāhi ṣallā allāhu ʿalayhi wa-sallama fī qawlihi al-zāhidu man lam yansa al-ghabra wa-al-balāʾa wa-āthara mā yabqā ʿalā mā yafnā wa-lam yaʿudda ghadan min ayyāmihi wa-ʿadda nafsahu fī al-mawtā
sentences.l: He said to me: The Messenger of God, God bless him and give him peace, has made it clear, in his saying: The ascetic is the one who does not forget the dust and the trial, and who prefers what remains to what perishes, and does not count tomorrow among his days, and counts himself among the dead.
sentences.i: He answered, “The Messenger of God, God bless him and give him peace, has made it plain: the ascetic is one who does not forget the dust and the trial, who prefers what lasts to what passes away, who does not count on tomorrow as one of his days, and who counts himself among the dead.”
sentences.n: The print has الغبر والبلاء, “the dust (or remainder) and the trial”, perhaps for القبر والبلى, “the grave and decay”; it is vocalised as printed. وعلّ نفسه is printed with lām; read as وعدّ نفسه, “and counts himself”.

sentences.t: وَقِيلَ إِنَّ أَبَاذَرٍّ كَانَ يَقُولُ الْفَقْرُ أَحَبُّ إِلَيَّ مِنَ الْغِنَى وَالسَّقَمُ أَحَبُّ إِلَيَّ مِنَ الصِّحَّةِ
sentences.tr: wa-qīla inna abā dharrin kāna yaqūlu al-faqru aḥabbu ilayya mina al-ghinā wa-al-saqamu aḥabbu ilayya mina al-ṣiḥḥati
sentences.l: And it was said that Abū Dharr used to say: Poverty is dearer to me than wealth, and sickness is dearer to me than health.
sentences.i: It is said that Abū Dharr used to say, “Poverty is dearer to me than wealth, and sickness dearer to me than health.”

sentences.t: فَقَالَ بَعْضُ السَّامِعِينَ رَحِمَ اللَّهُ أَبَاذَرٍّ أَمَّا أَنَا فَأَقُولُ مَنِ اتَّكَلَ عَلَى حُسْنِ الِاخْتِيَارِ مِنَ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى رَضِيَ بِالْحَالَةِ الَّتِي اخْتَارَهَا اللَّهُ لَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla baʿḍu al-sāmiʿīna raḥima allāhu abā dharrin ammā anā fa-aqūlu mani ttakala ʿalā ḥusni al-ikhtiyāri mina allāhi taʿālā raḍiya bi-al-ḥālati allatī ikhtārahā allāhu lahu
sentences.l: Then one of the hearers said: May God have mercy on Abū Dharr. As for me, I say: Whoever relies on the goodness of the choice from God, exalted is He, is content with the state which God has chosen for him.
sentences.i: One of those listening said, “May God have mercy on Abū Dharr. As for me, I say that whoever relies on the goodness of God’s choice is content with whatever state God has chosen for him.”

sentences.t: وَقَالَ بَعْضُ الثِّقَاتِ صَلَّى بِنَا ابْنُ أَبِي أَوْفَى صَلَاةَ الصُّبْحِ فَقَرَأَ يَا أَيُّهَا الْمُدَّثِّرُ حَتَّى بَلَغَ قَوْلَهُ تَعَالَى فَإِذَا نُقِرَ فِى النَّاقُورِ فَخَرَّ مَيِّتًا
sentences.tr: wa-qāla baʿḍu al-thiqāti ṣallā bi-nā ibnu abī awfā ṣalāta al-ṣubḥi fa-qaraʾa yā ayyuhā al-muddaththiru ḥattā balagha qawlahu taʿālā fa-idhā nuqira fī al-nāqūri fa-kharra mayyitan
sentences.l: And one of the trustworthy said: Ibn Abī Awfā led us in the dawn prayer, and he recited “O you, the wrapped-one,” until he reached His saying, exalted is He, “For when the trumpet is sounded,” and he fell down dead.
sentences.i: One of the trustworthy told how Ibn Abī Awfā led them in the dawn prayer and recited “O you who are wrapped in your cloak,” until he reached the words of the Almighty, “For when the trumpet is sounded,” and he fell down dead.
sentences.n: The Qurʾānic passage is sūrat al-Muddaththir 74:1 and 74:8. The print marks نُقر with ḍamma and خرّ with shadda; the marks are kept.

sentences.t: وَيُرْوَى أَنَّ ثَابِتًا الْبُنَانِيَّ بَكَى حَتَّى كَادَتْ أَنْ تَذْهَبَ عَيْنَاهُ فَجَاؤَا بِرَجُلٍ يُعَالِجُهُ قَالَ أُعَالِجُهُ بِشَرْطِ أَنْ يُطَا وِعَنِي قَلٰ ثَابِتٌ فِي أَيِّ شَيْءٍ قَلٰ الطَّبِيبُ فِي أَنْ لَا تَبْكِيَ قَلٰ ثَابِتٌ فَمَا فَضْلُ عَيْنَايَ إِنْ لَمْ تَبْكِيَا
sentences.tr: wa-yurwā anna thābitan al-bunāniyya bakā ḥattā kādat an tadhhaba ʿaynāhu fa-jāʾū bi-rajulin yuʿālijuhu qāla uʿālijuhu bi-sharṭi an yuṭāwiʿanī qala thābitun fī ayyi shayʾin qala al-ṭabību fī an lā tabkiya qala thābitun fa-mā faḍlu ʿaynāya in lam tabkiyā
sentences.l: And it is related that Thābit al-Bunānī wept until his eyes were about to go; so they brought a man to treat him. He said: I will treat him on condition that he obey me. Thābit said: In what thing? The physician said: In that you not weep. Thābit said: Then what is the merit of my two eyes if they do not weep?
sentences.i: It is related that Thābit al-Bunānī wept until his eyes were almost lost, and they brought a man to treat him. The man said, “I will treat him on condition that he does as I say.” “In what?” asked Thābit. “That you do not weep,” said the physician. “Then what good are my eyes,” said Thābit, “if they do not weep?”
sentences.n: The print spells يطاوعني as يطا وعني (with a space) and قال as قل throughout; both are read as intended. كادت is feminine for “his eyes”; فضل عيناي is printed with the nominative dual, as the print has it. جاؤا is the edition’s spelling of جاؤوا.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ رَجُلٌ لِمُحَمَّدِ بْنِ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ أَوْصِنِي
sentences.tr: wa-qāla rajulun li-muḥammadi bni ʿabdi allāhi awṣinī
sentences.l: And a man said to Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh: Counsel me.
sentences.i: A man said to Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh, “Give me counsel.”

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَ زَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka shahra zāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: Then morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent, leaving the permitted tale unsaid.
